blocks.text: 7. To the crocodile. Solinus: By natural providence it marks out a place for its nest. 8. To worms. Thus Pliny, book 11, ch. 28, says that little worms nest in dung. 9. To the gnat, the fly, the bee, the wasp and the hornet. Lucian in the Praise of the Fly: Νεοττίαν δὲ, ἢ καλιὰν, [col. 414] [III, 202] οὐκ ἐνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο [Neottian de, ē kalian, ouk eni topō katestēsato]; But it has not set up its nest, or little nest, in a single place. And in the Icaromenippus: Ἅπαντα διαγινώσκεις τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς· τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, τὰ θηρία, μικροῦ δεῖν, τὰς τῶν ἐμπίδων νεοττίας [Hapanta diaginōskeis ta epi gēs; tous anthrōpous, ta thēria, mikrou dein, tas tōn empidōn neottias]; You discern all things that are on earth: men, beasts and, I might almost say, the nests of gnats. Josephus on Samson, Antiquities, book 5, ch. 10: Ἐπιτυγχάνει σμήνει μελισσῶν, ἐν τῷ στήθει τοῦ λέοντος ἐκείνου νενοσσευκότων [Epitynchanei smēnei melissōn, en tō stēthei tou leontos ekeinou nenosseukotōn]; He came upon a swarm of bees which had nested in the breast of that lion. The Chaldee paraphrase of Iudic. XIV, 8: והא קנא דדבריתא בפגרא דאריא, And behold, a nest of bees in the carcass of the lion! And the Arabic: واذا في صدر الاسد نحل قد عششت هناك وقد سال العسل من عش النحل [wa-idhā fī ṣadr al-asad naḥl qad ʿashshashat hunāka wa-qad sāla al-ʿasal min ʿushsh al-naḥl] And behold, in the breast of the lion bees which had nested there, and honey was flowing from the bees' nest. So too 1 Sam. XIV, 26. The honey was flowing down من عش النحل [min ʿushsh al-naḥl] from the bees' nest. And the Chaldee again in the following verse: He stretched out the end of the staff that he had in his hand and dipped it בקינא דדובשא, in the nest of honey. Virgil, Georgics book 4, on bees:
They cherish their offspring and their nests. — —

Pliny, book 11, ch. 21: Wasps make their nests of mud up on high, and their wax in them; hornets in caves and underground. And again: The wasps that are called ichneumons kill one kind of spider, called the phalangium, and carry it into their nests. Likewise, on hornets: In spring they make nests, generally with four doors, in which the workers are bred. When these have been reared, they then build other, larger nests, in which they bring forth the future mothers. And ch. 22, on silkworms: They form nests of mud in the shape of salt, fixed to a stone, of such hardness that they can hardly be pierced with spear-points. Epiphanius, Heresy 44, on the kind of wasp they call ζώπυρον [zōpyron]: Ἐπὰν δέ τις διερχόμενος τὸν αὐτοῦ φωλεὸν, ἢ καλιὰν, καθέλοι [Epan de tis dierchomenos ton autou phōleon, ē kalian, katheloi]; If a traveller destroys its lair and nest. The ζώπυρον [zōpyron] is in Chaldee זיבורא zibbora, and the Arabs' زنبور [zunbūr] zanbur, of which Damir says: يتخذ عشه تحت الارض [yattakhidhu ʿushshahu taḥta al-arḍ] It takes its nest for itself under the earth. 10. To ants. Thus in the Talmudic tractate Nedarim you read קיני דשומשמני, nests of ants. And in Horus, book 2, ch. 60: Τιθεμένων (νυκτερίδος) τῶν πτερῶν εἰς τὴν νεοσσίαν τῶν μυρμήκων, οὐ προσέρχεται αὐτῶν τις [Tithemenōn (nykteridos) tōn pterōn eis tēn neossian tōn myrmēkōn, ou proserchetai autōn tis]; When a bat's wings are placed at the nests of ants, not one of them comes out. And Apuleius, book 8: In whose very rotten trunk the nests of the ants dwelling there were swarming (var. bubbling). 11. To mice and other small animals. Minucius Felix: Mice, etc., unless you drive them away, nest in the very mouth of your god. And Arnobius, book 6: Do you not see that under the bases (var. hollows) of these images geckos, shrews, mice and light-shunning cockroaches make their nests [III, 203] and dwell? 12. To locusts. Hence, when David complains that he has been shaken off like a locust, Psalm. CIX, 23, Kimchi and Aben Ezra observe that it refers to a locust שאין לו קן, which has no nest. And Damir, after saying that the locust, when about to bring forth, beats the hardest rocks with its tail until they open in a crack, and lays its eggs in that crack, adds: فيكون له كالافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا [fa-yakūnu lahu ka-l-ufḥūṣ wa-yakūnu ḥāḍinan lahā wa-murabbiyan] And (this crack) serves them as a nest, in which they cherish and rear their young. 13. Finally, it is certain that nests are not seldom attributed to serpents. Cic., On Divination, book 2: That there was a snake in the cradle is not so wonderful, especially in Solonium (which is a plain in the territory of Lanuvium), where snakes are wont to nest by the hearth. Some wrongly read nundinari [to hold market]. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 16: Ὅταν ἐπὶ [col. 415] τὴν πηγὴν τὸ ὕδωρ πιεῖν ἔλθῃ ὁ ὄφις, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται [Hotan epi tēn pēgēn to hydōr piein elthē ho ophis, ou pherei ton ion, alla ge apheis auton en tē neottia, houtō katharos poreuetai]; When the serpent comes to the spring to drink, it does not carry its poison with it, but, having left it in its nest, approaches thus pure. In its nest, that is, ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ [en tō phōleō], in its lair, as the same author has it in the Heresy of the Ophites, ch. 8. R. Selomo, explaining what the hole of the asp is in Esa. XI, 8, says that it is a hole in the earth שהנחש מקנן בתוכו, in the midst of which the serpent nests. And the Arabic translator in the same place has for hole of the asp عش الافاعي [ʿushsh al-afāʿī], the nest of vipers.
